items.prompt:
The table shows development indicators for two countries (approximate figures):

| indicator | Country A | Country B |
|---|---|---|
| GNI per head / US$ | 780 | 44 000 |
| life expectancy / years | 63 | 83 |
| infant mortality / deaths per 1000 live births | 46 | 3 |
| literacy rate / per cent of adults | 55 | 99 |

Describe the differences the table shows between Country A and Country B.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows Country B far more developed than Country A on every indicator, and the indicators agree with one another. Country B's life expectancy is 83 years against Country A's 63 years, a gap of 83 - 63 = 20 years. Country A's infant mortality is 46 deaths per 1000 live births, many times Country B's 3 per 1000. GNI per head is about 780 US dollars in Country A against 44 000 US dollars in Country B, and its literacy rate of 55 per cent means barely half its adults can read and write, compared with 99 per cent in Country B. So the pattern runs one way through the whole table: A is a low-income, less developed country and B a high-income, highly developed one.
marking_guidance: Reading: the overall pattern read from the table - B higher on every indicator, so the two countries sit far apart in development (1 mark).
Values: paired figures from the table with their units, so each statement is backed by a value - life expectancy, infant mortality, GNI per head or literacy (1 mark).
Meaning: the indicators read as a set - their agreement means the table is interpreted as a whole, not listed row by row (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use a variety of indicators to assess the level of development of a country

items.prompt: The infant mortality rate of one country was 52 deaths per 1000 live births in 2012 and 34 deaths per 1000 live births in 2022. Calculate the fall in the infant mortality rate between 2012 and 2022.
items.canonical_answer: 52 - 34 = 18. The infant mortality rate fell by 18 deaths per 1000 live births between 2012 and 2022.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the working 52 - 34 = 18 gives the method; the final answer is a fall of 18, and the unit is deaths per 1000 live births - an answer without its unit is incomplete.

items.prompt: Asked to describe a country's level of development from a table of indicators, a learner writes only: "Life expectancy 63 years. Infant mortality 46. Literacy 55 per cent." Explain the error in this answer.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has used statistics alone: a list of figures is not a description of development, because nothing is said about the pattern they form or what they mean. The correct answer states the pattern in words and supports each statement with a figure from the resource, with its unit - for example, that a life expectancy of 63 years is low, which suggests the country is less developed. The test is whether there is a statement and a figure that backs it: here every figure stands alone and no statement is made at all.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - statistics alone, with no statement of the pattern, and in fact figures by themselves describe nothing.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - describe the pattern in words, then back each statement with a figure and its unit from the resource.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use a variety of indicators to assess the level of development of a country

items.prompt: Asked why a transnational corporation runs so many of its stores in Namibia, a learner writes: "It creates jobs for Namibians, and the prices are lower than at other shops." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has described the effects of the corporation - jobs created, prices offered - instead of the reasons it operates there. Location reasons are not the same as impacts: a transnational corporation operates in Namibia because the market is there, in growing towns with many shoppers; because neighbouring countries are reached easily from Namibia's roads and ports; and because retail investment has been welcomed. Jobs and prices are what the company does once located there, not why it is there. The test is whether the answer says why it is there, or what it does there.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - effects such as jobs and prices are not the same as location reasons, and in fact the question asked why it operates there.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - location reasons such as the market, transport links or government incentives.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use a variety of indicators to assess the level of development of a country

items.prompt: Describe two features of the differences in development within Namibia.
items.canonical_answer: Jobs and services concentrate in Windhoek and the coastal towns of the Erongo region, so incomes there are higher than in most rural areas. The north-eastern regions, such as Kavango East and Zambezi, record the country's highest poverty rates (2015/16 survey pattern), and income distribution as a whole is among the most unequal in the world, with a Gini coefficient around 0.56 (2015/16 figure).
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all, each a fact about the named country - the contrast between the capital or the coast and the north-east, or the measured income inequality - not a general point about inequality.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and explain inequalities between and within countries

items.prompt: Explain why some countries have stayed less developed than others.
items.canonical_answer: Several causes work together. A landlocked position, deserts or mountains can make trade costly, which deters industry because goods are hard to export. A colonial history often left countries exporting one raw material, so their earnings swing with world prices. Diseases such as malaria burden hot, wet regions, which keeps workers and investors away. Political instability and war deter investment, and because investment is what creates jobs, its absence locks in poverty. Debt repayments can also swallow government money that would otherwise fund schools and health care, so each generation starts poorer.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: a cause given with how it works - physical barriers to trade, single-crop colonial economies, disease, instability or debt - because a cause named without its effect is not an explanation.
Award any three developed causes; the mark is for the causal link, so credit answers that state the effect explicitly.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and explain inequalities between and within countries

items.prompt:
The table shows GNI per head, in US dollars, for two countries (approximate figures):

| year | 1995 | 2005 | 2015 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Country C | 900 | 1 400 | 2 600 | 4 100 |
| Country D | 21 000 | 27 500 | 35 000 | 44 000 |

Describe the trend the table shows in the difference between the two countries.
items.canonical_answer: The overall trend is that the gap between the two countries widened across the thirty years, even though both grew richer. In 1995 the difference in GNI per head was 21 000 - 900 = 20 100 US dollars; by 2025 it was 44 000 - 4 100 = 39 900 US dollars, so the gap roughly doubled. Country C grew faster in proportion to its starting point - its GNI per head more than quadrupled, from 900 to 4 100 US dollars - but because Country D started so far ahead, the absolute difference kept widening all the same.
marking_guidance: Reading: the overall trend stated first - a widening gap across the whole period, read from the table (1 mark).

Values: the difference worked from the figures for the first and last years, so the trend statement is backed by values (1 mark); the recognition that both countries rose, which means the trend is about the difference and not the level (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Identify and explain inequalities between and within countries

items.prompt: Asked to describe the trend in a country's GNI per head between 1995 and 2025, a learner writes: "In 1995 it was 900 US dollars, and in 2025 it was 4 100 US dollars." Explain what is missing from this answer.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has compared two individual years without stating the overall trend. A trend is what the whole series does across the whole period - here, GNI per head rose steadily, more than quadrupling between 1995 and 2025. The correct answer states the overall trend first, then supports it with figures such as the 1995 and 2025 values, and notes any exception. The test is whether the answer says in one sentence what the whole table shows; quoting two years is not the same as describing a trend.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the mistake named - two single years are compared and no overall trend is stated, which is not the same as a trend.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - state the overall trend first (rising), then the supporting figures and any exception.

objective_titles: Identify and explain inequalities between and within countries

items.prompt: State what is meant by the tertiary sector.
items.canonical_answer: The tertiary sector is the part of the economy that provides services rather than goods: work such as teaching, nursing, transport, banking and shop work.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the meaning of the term: the sector that provides services, with an illustration of it - an answer about making goods describes a different sector.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Classify production into different sectors and give illustrations of each

items.prompt: Describe two illustrations of primary sector work.
items.canonical_answer: Fishing for pilchards off Walvis Bay, where crews take wild fish from the sea. Mining copper around Tsumeb in northern Namibia, where ore is cut from the ground. Both are primary because they extract raw materials directly from nature rather than making or selling anything.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per illustration, 2 in all, each a fact that names a primary activity - extraction of a raw material, not its manufacture or its sale - so each point must identify what is being taken from nature.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Classify production into different sectors and give illustrations of each

items.prompt: Describe the employment structure typical of a low-income country.
items.canonical_answer: Most workers - often more than half, and in some countries two thirds or more - are in the primary sector, mainly farming with hand tools. The secondary share is small, because industry is limited, and the tertiary share is small too, since few people can afford many services. The structure is dominated by primary work.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the dominance of primary work (with a share or a description of the type of work), or the small secondary and tertiary shares - each stated as a fact about the employment structure.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain how the proportions employed in each sector vary according to the level of development

items.prompt: Explain why the proportion of workers in the primary sector falls as a country develops.
items.canonical_answer: Machines and better seed raise each farmer's output, so fewer farmers can feed the whole country, which releases workers from the land. As investment builds factories and services, those jobs pay more than farming, so workers move to towns, where secondary and tertiary work grows. Rising incomes then create demand for services - shops, transport, health care - so the tertiary share keeps climbing. The primary proportion falls not because less food is produced but because each worker produces more of it and because other kinds of work have grown faster.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: mechanisation raising output per farmer, so fewer farmers are needed; better-paid secondary and tertiary jobs drawing workers to towns, which causes the shift; rising incomes creating service jobs - each point is how the shift happens, so credit the mechanism rather than the fact alone.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain how the proportions employed in each sector vary according to the level of development

items.prompt:
The table shows the employment structure of three countries (share of workers, per cent):

| sector | Country E, low income | Country F, middle income | Country G, high income |
|---|---|---|---|
| primary | 63 | 33 | 3 |
| secondary | 14 | 31 | 21 |
| tertiary | 23 | 36 | 76 |

Describe the pattern the table shows between employment structure and level of development.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows employment structure shifting steadily with development. The primary share falls from 63 per cent in the low-income country to 33 per cent in the middle-income one and just 3 per cent in the high-income one. The tertiary share rises in the same direction, from 23 to 36 to 76 per cent. The secondary share behaves differently: it is largest in the middle-income country at 31 per cent, which means manufacturing grows first and then declines as a share once services dominate. So the pattern is primary falling, tertiary rising, and secondary peaking in between - and the shares, not job totals, are what the table records.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table across the three countries - primary falls and tertiary rises as development rises (1 mark).

Values: the percentages used to support each statement, so the figures carry the description (1 mark); the secondary share's peak in the middle-income country noticed, which means the table is read as a whole (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain how the proportions employed in each sector vary according to the level of development

items.prompt: Reading that "primary 63 per cent" of a country's workers are in the primary sector, a learner writes: "So the country has 63 primary workers." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The figure is a share, not a total: 63 per cent means 63 of every 100 workers farm, mine, fish or work in forestry - it says nothing about how many workers the country has in all. The number of primary jobs could be thousands or millions; employment structure records the share of workers in each sector, not the count. The learner has confused the share of jobs with the number of jobs. The test is whether the figure is a percentage or a total, and which sector the job belongs to.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a percentage is not the same as a count, and in fact 63 per cent describes a share of all workers.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - employment structure is the share of workers in each sector, so the country holds 63 primary workers per 100, not 63 in total.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain how the proportions employed in each sector vary according to the level of development

items.prompt: Describe two benefits globalisation has brought to low-income countries.
items.canonical_answer: Jobs and wages: transnational corporations have built garment, shoe and electronics factories in low-income countries, because labour costs less there, so wages have arrived where few formal jobs existed before. Wider markets: the same links let a grower or workshop sell to buyers in many countries instead of one local market, which means a chance to earn export income. Cheaper imports also raise living standards, because consumer goods cost less than home-made equivalents.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, 2 in all, each developed with its consequence - jobs created because labour costs less, or export markets opened - so the benefit is taken to what it means, not just listed.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the process of globalisation, and consider its impacts

items.prompt: Describe two problems globalisation can bring.
items.canonical_answer: Job losses in old industrial regions: because production can move to wherever costs are lowest, factories can close where wages are higher, so whole towns can lose their main employer. Loss of profits and control: a transnational corporation's profits flow to its headquarters country, so part of the wealth a host country creates leaves it, and because the head office makes the decisions, the host country has little say over what happens in the plant.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem, 2 in all, each developed with its consequence - closures because production moves abroad, or profits leaving the host country - so the problem is linked to what it means for the people affected.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the process of globalisation, and consider its impacts

items.prompt: A country attracted clothing factories by keeping wages low and by building an industrial park beside its port. Suggest how far you would judge globalisation to have benefited this country.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that globalisation has benefited the country, but partly and with a risk attached. The evidence for: the factories created jobs beside the port where few formal jobs existed before, and export income has lifted wages and government revenue, so the gain is real. The evidence against: the jobs depend on staying cheap, because the same global links let the companies move on if wages rise, and the profits flow to the headquarters countries. So the better judgement is benefit with dependence - worthwhile while it lasts, fragile in the long run - which means the country should use the income to build skills and services that stay.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision on how far the benefit goes - benefited, but partly and with a risk (1 mark).
Because: the reasons weighed - jobs and export income against dependence on low wages, since the factories can move on (1 mark).
Evidence: the reasons tied to this example's features - the port-side industrial park and the low wages - so the judgement is justified by the situation given (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the process of globalisation, and consider its impacts

items.prompt:
The table shows where the jeans sold by one large Windhoek shop were made:

| year | made in Namibia | made in other countries |
|---|---|---|
| 2005 | 26 per cent | 74 per cent |
| 2015 | 14 per cent | 86 per cent |
| 2024 | 8 per cent | 92 per cent |

Describe what the table shows about where the shop's goods come from.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the shop's jeans becoming steadily less likely to be made in Namibia: the share made locally falls from 26 per cent in 2005 to 8 per cent in 2024, while the share made in other countries rises to 92 per cent. So the shop's supply shifted almost entirely to producers abroad over the twenty years, which is globalisation seen in one shop's stock: the jeans link the shop's customers to factories in many countries, and the falling local share suggests Namibian clothing manufacture could not match the imported prices.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - the local share falls and the overseas share rises across the period (1 mark).

Values: the trend supported with the percentages for the first and last years, so the figures back the statement (1 mark); the shift linked to globalisation and its cause, which means the resource is interpreted, not just summarised (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the process of globalisation, and consider its impacts

items.prompt: For Shoprite, the South African food retail group, describe two features of its global links.
items.canonical_answer: Scale and spread: the group runs more than 3 000 stores in about 15 African countries from its Cape Town head office (2020s figures, approximate), which links suppliers, workers and shoppers across the continent through one company. Sourcing: goods move through the group's large distribution centres in South Africa to stores in Namibia and other countries, so a Windhoek shelf connects Namibian shoppers to farms and factories in several countries at once.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all, each a fact about the named corporation's links - the store network across countries, or the South African distribution centres feeding Namibian stores - not a general point about retailers.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of a transnational corporation and its global links

items.prompt: Shoprite opened its first store outside South Africa in Windhoek in 1990 and now trades from more than 30 Namibian towns. Explain why a food retailer headquartered in South Africa operates on this scale in Namibia.
items.canonical_answer: The market: Namibia's towns hold hundreds of thousands of shoppers who buy food every week, so the country offers a large, reliable retail market close to the company's existing supply lines. Timing and position: Namibia's independence in 1990 opened a stable neighbouring market, and because the company already ran South African stores and distribution centres, extending north was a small step for a large gain. Supply and costs: the existing distribution centres mean stock reaches Namibian shelves cheaply, and local staff and local suppliers - bakers, dairies, vegetable growers - keep costs and prices sensible. Each reason explains why the stores are there, not what they do once there.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each reason tied to this example because a reason must explain presence in Namibia: the size and closeness of the market; the 1990 opening after independence, so the political moment mattered; the existing South African supply lines, which means extension was cheap; the local staff and suppliers, so the stores run at sensible cost.
Answers that describe jobs or prices in the stores describe effects, not reasons, so they earn no credit here.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of a transnational corporation and its global links

items.prompt: For a named transnational corporation you have studied, describe its global links and explain how they affect one country where it operates. [7]
items.canonical_answer:
Shoprite Holdings is a food retail transnational corporation headquartered at Brackenfell in Cape Town, South Africa, and listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. Its links reach Namibia directly: it entered the country in 1990, opening its first store outside South Africa in Windhoek, and by the 2020s traded from more than 30 Namibian towns (approximate figures).
The links affect Namibia in both directions. Goods: most stock moves through the group's distribution centres in South Africa, so Namibian shelves are supplied cheaply and reliably, though the stores also buy from Namibian bakers, dairies and vegetable growers. People: the stores employ Namibian staff in every town they serve. Money: wages and supplier payments stay in Namibia, but part of the profit flows to the group's shareholders outside the country, because buying and pricing are decided at the Cape Town head office.
The judgement is that Namibia gains affordable food and steady jobs from the corporation's links, while a share of the wealth the shops create leaves the country - the same links seen from two ends.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about transnational corporations, with no named example or only general points about shops or jobs.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named corporation, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Shoprite, its 1990 entry into Namibia, the Brackenfell head office, the South African distribution centres, more than 30 Namibian towns - covering both the links and their effects.

items.prompt:
The table shows development indicators for four countries (approximate figures):

| indicator | Country A | Country B | Country C | Country D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GNI per head / US$ | 560 | 1 900 | 9 200 | 44 000 |
| life expectancy / years | 61 | 69 | 74 | 83 |
| infant mortality / deaths per 1000 live births | 58 | 27 | 14 | 3 |
| literacy rate / per cent of adults | 48 | 71 | 91 | 99 |

(a) Identify the country where a newborn can expect to live the longest. [1]
(b) Describe two differences between Country A and Country D shown by the table. [2]
(c) Suggest two reasons for the difference in infant mortality between Country A and Country D. [3]
(d) Suggest two indicators, not shown in the table, that could be used to compare these countries' development. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Country D.
(b) GNI per head is about 78 times higher in Country D, at 44 000 US dollars against 560 US dollars. Life expectancy is 83 years in Country D against 61 years in Country A, a difference of 83 - 61 = 22 years, and Country A's infant mortality of 58 deaths per 1000 live births is many times Country D's 3 per 1000.
(c) Country A's infants face poorer health care, so birth complications and early illnesses go untreated. Many families in Country A also lack safe water and enough food, so infants weaken and diseases such as diarrhoea kill more easily - dirty water, infection, and death run as a chain.
(d) Access to safe water; the number of doctors per 1000 people (also creditable: the birth rate, or the proportion of children in school).
marking_guidance: Resource: parts (a) and (b) are read from the table's data - 1 mark for Country D; 2 marks for two differences, each backed with paired figures and their units.
Marks: part (c) is worth 3 marks - two reasons for the infant mortality gap (health care, nutrition, safe water), with one developed along its chain of effects for the third mark.
Figures: part (d) is worth 2 marks - two named indicators not in the table, each a recognised measure of development; credit evidence such as safe water, doctors per 1000 people or the birth rate.
